Different explanatory reasons do not make the thing itself many; they add reasons from outside it. People commonly think that different defining features do make the thing itself many. But careful thought and proof show that there is a difference between features that differ in meaning and features that differ in reality and existence. Every concept differs from other concepts in meaning, but some concepts can still be one in reality. “Existence” and “being an individual,” for example, differ in meaning but are one in reality. “Knowing” and “being known” differ in meaning, but can belong to one simple being. God’s knowledge and power differ in meaning, yet are one in His being, as we have explained.

Some differences really do give a thing distinguishable parts or powers. Some differ from one another but are not direct opposites—for example, shape, size, color, taste, smell, heat, movement, and relation. Others are directly opposed: black and white, knowledge and ignorance, earlier and later in relation to one thing, or existence and non-existence. A further principle applies to all these features, whether essential or added: the reason why a thing has one feature is not the same as the reason why it has another. A person is not rational because they can write, nor able to speak because they are an animal. If it were otherwise, every animal could reason, every human being would already be a writer, and every shaped thing would be moving.

This is true both in existence and in meaning. Being able to know and being something that can be known do not mean the same thing; otherwise they would be two words for one meaning. Earlier writers did not always distinguish the two kinds of difference. They said that a thing’s qualities cannot come from different respects unless still earlier, different causes explain them. But their point does not mean that one thing cannot have several qualities unless those qualities first multiply the thing itself. Opposed qualities are a special case: one thing cannot really have both sides of an opposition at once unless there is a real difference in its parts or powers. A difference created only by thought, such as dividing a human being into animal nature and rational nature, does not let the same thing be both knowing and ignorant, or both black and white. The two opposites must belong to two distinct things.

Other defining features, such as blackness and movement, can both belong to one natural thing. But this is possible only when they come from different powers or sources, whether or not those powers always act together. The plant and animal powers within a human being, for example, produce different kinds of action.

Another principle follows. A thing can have a quality in one respect or at one level without having it in every respect or at every level. If we say that Zayd exists, it is enough that he exists in some way; he need not exist through himself, without any cause. If we say Zayd is black, we do not mean he is black because he is human, a writer, knowledgeable, generous, or brave. Those features have nothing to do with his color. He is not black in those respects, but that does not stop the statement “Zayd is black” from being true. A thing is established if it exists in any way; it is absent only if it is absent in every way.

We can now say this: if a subject is simple in every respect, whatever is true of it must be true of it in every respect and at every level of reality.

The principles we have recalled are enough for reason to show that the One, the pure First Reality, and anything considered simply as one, can produce only one thing insofar as it is one. A many-sided thing cannot produce many effects as many, nor can two first effects come from it at once. One thing must come first, then another, until different respects and causes appear and the door to many good things opens. This principle may be one of the truths that a sound mind sees naturally. Yet those who oppose the people of truth have strongly denied it, so the way to wisdom will not open to them.

They also deny the existence of separate lights, intellectual beings, and forms that do not depend on matter, bodies, or dimensions. Their nature is too heavy to rise to another level and live near those who dwell in God’s holy sanctuary. They sit down with those who sit idle. Had they wanted to leave, they would have prepared for the journey; but God did not will their setting out, so they were held back and told, “Stay with those who stay behind.” They seem, in their hearts, to be enemies of spiritual beings and the angels brought near to God, even if they do not say so openly. God says: “Say, ‘Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel—he brought it down upon your heart by God’s permission.’” So the people of truth have tried to prove this claim decisively and answer objections, to protect those seeking truth from the doubts of people who deny spiritual beings and God’s action.

We also discussed an objection raised by a leading critic of philosophy, who used logic against its own master, and showed where the confusion lay.

Some mistaken thinkers have said that one pure being could have a single natural fit with two things, and that this one fit could make both come from it at once. I say that a bare denial can either be the denial of a whole statement—“It is not the case that A is B”—or it can be part of the statement itself, as in “A is not B.” In the first case, the statement only denies a claim. Once the subject exists, the two forms are always true or false together. For example, if “A is a human, not a horse” is true, then “A is not a horse” is true. So this kind of denial needs an existing subject that matches it. An affirmative statement joins its subject and predicate. The denial in “A is not a horse” therefore has to be grounded in the subject itself, especially when the statement says what the subject is, rather than merely describing it.

But God is not a being whose essence can be divided by analysis, as things may be one in reality yet contain several distinct features when we consider them. Second, the respect in which God produces the first intellect is the very same respect in which He produces all goodness and the whole order of the world. The first intellect contains the later order in a unified way, just as a thing’s defining form makes its parts one thing. We have shown that a thing is what it is through its form, not its matter. The form is the thing’s completion and true self. The intellect is, in a higher and simpler way, all the things that come after it.
